title: Clean on the outside (Luke 11:37–54)
hookLine: he eats with Pharisees and challenges religion that's all surface

cards: A Pharisee invites Jesus to dinner, and Luke shows him at Pharisees' tables more than once. The Pharisees in this scene care about holiness at the table itself: washing, tithing, cups and dishes.
So when the guest sits straight down without washing, the host is startled. The King James Bible says he "marvelled that he had not first washed before dinner."
And Jesus, at someone else's table, answers the look on his face.

teach.b: "Now do ye Pharisees make clean the outside of the cup and the platter; but your inward part is full of ravening and wickedness." Ravening means grabbing, greed.
It's a sharp thing to say at dinner, and Luke doesn't soften it. Then a riddle: "did not he that made that which is without make that which is within also?"
God made the cup's inside as well as its outside; you can't polish one and ignore the other.
His answer to how is surprising: give alms from what's within, and everything is clean. Generosity cleans the inside of the cup.
Then he names their careful tithing, a tenth of even mint and rue from the herb garden, and says they pass over justice and the love of God.
But listen to the end of the sentence: "these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone."

teach.h: DO BOTH: THE SMALL AND THE GREAT.
teach.b: He doesn't throw out the small faithful habits. He says do both. This is the language of Israel's own prophets, speaking to their own people.

teach.h: NOT TO LEAVE THE OTHER UNDONE.
teach.b: Micah asked what the Lord requires, and answered: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. It's an argument inside a family, and any church can hear it about itself.

And so a week on the road closes: wisdom given to little ones, a Samaritan who stopped, Martha and Mary, a short prayer, a friend knocking at midnight, a lamp in the eye, and now a cup that needs washing on both sides.

how: Some Christians pair outward practices, like grace before meals, tithing or fasting, with an inward examination of conscience, and the season of Lent joins fasting with prayer and almsgiving, the giving this passage names.

o: a tenth of crops given to God

games.q: what's inside Luke 11:37–54 — tap the pairs.
p: justice and the love of God

s: Jesus tells them tithing herbs doesn't matter
"these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone." he says do both.
Luke shows him at Pharisees' tables more than once, here and in chapters 7 and 14.
Jesus says giving alms makes the inside clean
give alms of what you have, and all things are clean to you.

games.q: you're the host. your honored guest sits down to eat without the ritual washing. what happens next in the story?
o: you say nothing, but you're startled, and he answers your look.
you wash his hands for him.
games.why: the Pharisee "marvelled that he had not first washed before dinner," and Jesus answers with the cup: the inside matters too.

practice: Pick up a cup or bowl near you, or picture one, and look into it; then turn your attention inward, to what sits inside you that nobody else can see: a grudge, a little greed, a story you tell yourself about someone.
Don't scrub at it; just name it honestly, and think of one generous thing you could give from the inside out: time, money, a kind word you've been holding back.
If you pray, offer that inside place to God as it is; if you don't, simply let it be named.

wordCard.voice: Alms. Jesus's answer to how the inside of the cup gets clean: give from what's within to the poor, and everything is made clean.

orig.note: Greek: from within, the inside. the part of the cup, and of a person, that Jesus says God also made.

carryVoice: Your line: the inside too. Generosity reaches where polish can't. A week on the road, closed.
